claims.text: The initial near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst has an ordered or only moderately disordered structure.
Adding earth-abundant transition metals or adjusting metal ratios during synthesis can transform the catalyst's active layer into a high-entropy spinel oxide.
Increasing the number of constituent transition metals increases configurational disorder in a spinel oxide.
Greater configurational disorder will optimize the distribution of metal cations in the spinel lattice.
Greater configurational disorder will produce an optimized concentration or distribution of surface oxygen vacancies.
Metal identity, valence, cation-site distribution, and surface oxygen-vacancy concentration influence spinel-oxide catalytic activity.
Configurational disorder promotes synergistic interactions among diverse active sites.
Increasing configurational disorder improves low-temperature CO oxidation activity.
The disordered surface stabilizes active sites against blocking by H2O and NO.
Increasing configurational disorder retards sintering and phase separation during long-term operation.
The modified catalyst will have a lower CO-oxidation T10 than the unmodified catalyst.
The modified catalyst will lose less activity during 14 hours of operation than the unmodified catalyst.
The modified catalyst will retain better performance in the presence of H2O and NO than the unmodified catalyst.
The proposed improvements will occur during transient automotive exhaust operation below 150 °C.
Performance under accelerated aging will predict durability over vehicle-lifetime mileage.
The activity, poisoning resistance, and durability improvements can be obtained without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
The modified catalyst would thereby meet stricter emissions standards.
